'''Péter István Mészáros''' (born 15 July 1943)<ref name="Hungarian Academy" /> is a Hungarian-Argentine theoretical astrophysicist,
best known for the [[Mészáros effect]]<ref name=":M74">Mészáros, P., "The behaviour of point masses in an expanding cosmological substratum", [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1974A%26A....37..225M/abstract Astronomy and Astrophysics, vol. 37, no. 2, Dec. 1974, p. 225-228]</ref> in cosmology and for his work on [[gamma-ray bursts]].<ref name=":MR97">Mészáros, P. and Rees, M.J., "Optical and Long-Wavelength Afterglow from Gamma-Ray Bursts", [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997ApJ...476..232M/abstract The Astrophysical Journal, Volume 476, Issue 1, Feb. 1997, pp. 232-237]</ref><ref name=":RM94">Rees, M.J. and Mészáros, P., "Unsteady Outflow Models for Cosmological Gamma-Ray Bursts", [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1994ApJ...430L..93R/abstract Astrophysical Journal Letters v.430, August 1994, pp.L93-L96]</ref>

== Life ==
Péter Mészáros was born in 1943 in [[Budapest]], Hungary, and grew up in [[Liège]], Belgium and [[Buenos Aires]], Argentina, where he did his undergraduate studies. He received his PhD in 1972 from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and after postdoctoral fellowships at [[Princeton University]] and [[Cambridge University]] he became a staff scientist at the [[Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics]]. He joined the [[Pennsylvania State University]] in 1983, where for ten years he was Head of the department of Astronomy and Astrophysics and Professor of Physics, being named Eberly Chair Professor.<ref>https://news.psu.edu/story/207785/2005/10/14/meszaros-named-holder-eberly-family-chair-astronomy-astrophysics Eberly Chair Professor</ref>

== Career ==
Mészáros is widely known in the astrophysical community for his papers on the relativistic fireball shock model of [[gamma ray bursts]] and their afterglows,<ref name=":MR97" /><ref name=":RM94" /> laying down the framework for the interplay between the jet dynamics and the external as well as internal shocks which determine the observational aspects of these sources. He is also known in the cosmological community for the [[Mészáros effect]],<ref name=":M74" /> or Mészáros equation, which quantifies the influence of [[dark matter]] in the evolution of the initial perturbations leading to large scale structures in [[cosmology]]. He was active in the study of the [[interstellar medium]] as well as the astrophysics of [[black holes]], and contributed broadly to the study of magnetized [[neutron stars]], e.g.<ref>{{Citation |last=Mészáros |first=Peter |title=High energy radiation from magnetized neutron stars |publisher=[[University of Chicago]] |location=Chicago |year=1992 |isbn=0-226-52093-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BVY7gEs11IYC}}, pp.1-531</ref> He served as the science-theory lead of the NASA [[Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory]] space mission. His current interests include calculations of theoretical models of cosmic high energy [[cosmic ray]] and [[neutrino]] sources, e.g.,<ref>Rachen, J.P. and Mészáros, P., "Photohadronic neutrinos from transients in astrophysical sources", [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1998PhRvD..58l3005R/abstract Physical Review D, Volume 58, Issue 12, 15 December 1998, id. 123005]</ref><ref>Murase, K., Kimura, S.S. and Mészáros, P., "Hidden Cores of Active Galactic Nuclei as the Origin of Medium-Energy Neutrinos: Critical Tests with the MeV Gamma-Ray Connection", [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020PhRvL.125a1101M/abstract Physical Review Letters, Volume 125, Issue 1, June 2020, id. 011101]</ref> as well as exploring various aspects of [[multimessenger astrophysics]].

== Positions ==
Mészáros is a Member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]] (2021),<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2021|title=NAS Fellows 2021|publisher=NAS|access-date=26 April 2021}}, entry in member directory:{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/peter-istvan-meszaros-0iv0dl/|title=Member Directory|access-date=4 July 2021|publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2010),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/166804/2010/06/08/academics/peter-meszaros-elected-2010-american-academy-fellow|title=Peter Meszaros elected as a 2010 American Academy Fellow &#124; Penn State University|website=news.psu.edu}}</ref>
Member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] (2010),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/166544/2010/06/21/academics/peter-meszaros-elected-member-hungarian-academy-sciences|title=Peter Meszaros elected a member of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences &#124; Penn State University|website=news.psu.edu}}</ref><ref name="Hungarian Academy">{{Cite web|url=https://mta.hu/koztestuleti_tagok?PersonId=19642|title=Az MTA köztestületének tagjai (en: Members of the Hungarian Academy)|access-date=4 July 2021|publisher=Magyar Tudomanyos Academia (en: Hungarian Academy of Sciences)|page=Mészáros Péter|language=Hungarian}}</ref>
Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (1996) and
Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] (2019).
He is the Eberly Chair Professor Emeritus of Astronomy and Astrophysics and of Physics at Penn State, and Director Emeritus of its Center for Multimessenger Astrophysics.<ref>http://sites.psu.edu/cmma
Penn State Center for Multimessenger Astrophysics</ref>
He is currently a member of the Space Studies Board of the National Academy of Sciences.<ref>https://www.nationalacademies.org/ssb/space-studies-board</ref>

== Awards ==
*2020 - Legacy Fellow, [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows|title=AAS Fellows|publisher=AAS|access-date=29 September 2020}}</ref>
*2013 – Einstein Professorship of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.psu.edu/news/einstein-professorship-awarded-peter-meszaros-chinese-academy/|title = Einstein Professorship Awarded to Péter Mészáros by the Chinese Academy &#124; Eberly College of Science}}</ref>
*2009 – Thomson Reuters scienceWATCH: Highest ranked in citations on gamma-ray bursts during 1999–2009<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://archive.sciencewatch.com/ana/st/gamma/09junGamMesz/|title=Peter Mészáros Interview - Special Topic of Gamma-ray Bursts - ScienceWatch.com|website=archive.sciencewatch.com}}</ref>
*2007 – [[Bruno Rossi Prize]] (shared with Neil Gehrels and the Swift team)
*2000 – [[Bruno Rossi Prize]] (shared with B. Paczynski and M.J. Rees)
*1999 – Fellow, [[John Simon Guggenheim Foundation]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/peter-i-meszaros/|title=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation &#124; Peter I. Mészáros |work=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation }}</ref>
*1996 - Fellow, [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_Physical_Society_Fellows_(1972–1997)|title=APS Fellows|website=American Physical Society}}</ref>{{Circular reference|date=November 2020}}
*1976 – First Prize, Gravity Research Foundation (shared with P. Kafka)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gravityresearchfoundation.org/year|title=Gravity Research Foundation|website=Gravity Research Foundation}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Mészáros is married to Deborah Mészáros, and they have an adult son, Andor Mészáros.
